en: Oṃ, homage to the glorious Vajrasattva!
He is the crest-jewel of the lords of the wheels moving within the subtle apertures of the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*;
he is as skillful as a sesame-seed splitter in producing the emanations of the Sugata;
his movement is one of constant bliss, and he bears a body that is the very house of the innate (*sahaja*).
May he whose form quivers, clothed in the sky of yoga, protect you day by day.
Her form is established upon the path of the thirty-three [gods];
her eyes are the mouth of the threefold liberation;
she holds the weapons of mindfulness, the hands, the peaks [of Mount Meru], the moon, and the senses.
May the goddess Sumaneśvarī protect you always.
Oṃ, homage to the glorious Vajrasattva.
The lord of the wheels moving within the subtle apertures of the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, adorned with the tilaka of the seed-syllable *siṃ*,
he is as skillful as a master illusionist in creating emanations of the Sugata;
his movement is one of constant bliss, and he bears a body that is the very womb of the co-emergent (*sahaja*).
May he whose form quivers, clothed in the raiment of yoga, protect you day after day.
Her body is established upon the path of the thirty-three [gods];
her eyes are the mouth of the threefold liberation and are beyond words; she holds the weapons of mindfulness, the hand-tips, the planets, the moon, and the senses.
May the auspicious Goddess of the Mind protect you always.
I salute that Lord of universal form, who is united with the illustrious celestial maiden, who perceives the fourfold bliss, who is the progenitor of the three worlds,
and who has descended through the sequence of the four seats (catuṣpīṭha) and is established within the four wheels (catuścakra).

The fourfold reality that has been proclaimed shall be written clearly by me. (0.2) Pure and seated upon a comfortable seat, having again worshipped the Sugatas and having visualized everything as empty, the wise one should contemplate what is taught in the Tantra. (1.1)
In a delightful gabled chamber, beautifully adorned upon the summit of Mount Meru,
one should meditate there on the mandala of the miraculous manifestation of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).
Situated at the soles of the feet is the wind element, its mandala shaped like a bow.
One should ascend from there step by step as far as the lotus of the navel.
[Therein is] the triangular fire-maṇḍala produced from the imperishable light;
by this, the entire universe, which is like space, has been burnt away.
Thereafter, one should contemplate the form according to the sequence of the ritual for the insignia-mantra:
seated upon a shimmering lion-throne, bearing the luster of the moon.
The yogin should constantly meditate on that which manifests as Jñānaḍākinī.
One should contemplate there a beautiful universal lotus situated between the fire and water [elements], with the first letter of the consonant groups radiating in all directions—
resembling snow, the kunda flower, and the moon, peaceful, and cool as a ray of light.
It is a great cloud of vibrating Buddhas, possessing the luster of jewels in all their forms;
it consists of the Goddess of Wisdom, is transparent, and has the beautiful form of the Dharmadhātu.
It is mounted upon a forest of its own serpents, overflowing with a stream that drenches one in nectar.
Form, sound, taste, smell, and the sphere of mental objects (dharmadhātu);
likewise, the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
the six consciousnesses, the primary elements, and the derivative elements consisting of the five aggregates.
For all these beings in the world, both stationary and moving, arise from that.
In the eastern direction, in the north, is the first [vowel]; the second begins with *svara*.
Up to the tenth is in the western direction, and its end is on the southern petal.
One should place the Ḍākinī of terrible form and the Vetālī Śvapacā in the cardinal direction;
and having placed the Siṃhī, Vyāghrī, Jambukī, and Pecikā in the intermediate directions—
one white, one yellow, one red, and the fourth dark blue— respectively.
In the corners, one should visualize those of mixed complexion born of neuter beings.
(1.13) They have one face and two arms, are fierce, and are adorned with divine ornaments;
they possess three eyes, exhibit a smile mixed with wrath, and hold a khaṭvāṅga staff and a skull-bowl. (1.14)
In the intermediate directions on the left are the goddesses, their hands holding the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) and nooses;
in their right hands, they hold the *khaṭvāṅga*, the battle-axe, and the indestructible staff.
These goddesses have crowns of vajras and are beautifully clad in elephant hides.
And they have human skins as upper garments and are colored by the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa).
In the four cardinal directions are the elephant, the peacock, the swan, and the servant;
the lion, the thunderbolt-faced one, and Caṇḍī; and likewise the jackal in the intermediate directions.
The Ḍākinī, Dīpinī, Cūṣiṇī, and Kambojī, each with her own hand-symbol,
should be meditated upon as mounted upon the sun-discs of corpses, colored according to their respective domains.
They are characterized by the mirror-like wisdom, the wisdom of equality, the wisdom of discernment, and the purity of accomplishment.
They are perfected as the forms of the Buddhas and sealed by the lords of their respective families.
As for the external cultivation of the mandala,
this is the form of the body resulting from that cultivation.
That which was previously mentioned is indeed the seed-syllable, the primordial vowel; one meditates upon it in the form of a drop (bindu).
One whose self is absorbed in yoga through this meditation shall accomplish all perfections (siddhis).
One whose mantra-self has not been propitiated is not capable of performing the ritual action.
The yogi should meditate upon that [deity] until a clear vision is attained;
having obtained the sign, he shall then swiftly and forever attain both accomplishment and liberation.
He who, with a concentrated mind, properly blocks his nose, mouth, ears, and eyes with his two hands, beholds the *Yogabindu*.
When [the breath] is transformed into drops within the wheels of air, fire, earth, water, and space, [he beholds it]. 1.23–24ab.
Having understood its characteristics, one should employ it according to the specific rite:
with white [sindūra], peace (śānti) is accomplished; with yellow or red, nourishment (pauṣṭika);
with black, disease is produced; and with grey, expulsion (uccāṭana) and killing (māraṇa) are effected.
Having placed both hands upon the secret place at the base of the stūpa,
and having seen the syllable *kaṣa* there, one who is well-composed should press it. With his gaze fixed on the tip of the nose, he beholds the deity of wind situated at the navel.

Having firmly established the emptiness of form, one should perform the supreme binding of the mind. Then, through the yoga of one's own tutelary deity, one should accumulate Vairocana and the others, beginning with Sva, together with the five Buddhas, by means of the necklace and the swing.
The final of the sibilants (ha) with two dots (the visarga), adorned by the ninth [letter] (na), and again the letter *ī* situated in fire (*ra*)—with these one should empower the fluids.
*Oṃ aṃ hūṃ svāhā*. This is to be recited. 1.29–31.
Haḥ Hoḥ Hrīḥ! The Empowerment. 1.32–33: A Ā Āṃ Āṃ Āḥ | Ṛṃ =Ṛṃ Ḷṃ =Ḷṃ |
phuṃ pheṃ phoṃ phriṃ | 1.34 These are the seed-syllables (bīja) of the maṇḍala-circle. || 1.35 [The syllable] situated in the fire-maṇḍala within the wind [element].
Having visualized all the bodily constituents within the skull-cup as having the form of liquid moonlight,
one then beholds the image of a lotus falling from the sky.
Padmeśvara, who possesses the luster of beautiful gold;
Vairocana, known as Gandhapaya;
Āsvādavajreśvara, and Vajrapāṇi.
The three gods should also be sustained by means of the threefold [method]. 1.37 Having visualized the form of Vahni at the navel,
radiant and emitting a web of shimmering rays;
One who mentally offers a pure oblation situated in the sun is not defiled.
Thus ends the first chapter: the reality of the *bindu* (the point), consisting of the mantra for the contemplation of the self-throne fashioned from the signs of the internal self (*ādhyātmika*).
Having compressed the downward-moving breath (apāna-vāyu) and bound it, one should direct it upward;

having steadied the "swinging necklace" (hārādola) and meditated upon the embodiment of knowledge, [one perceives] the channel shaped like a plantain flower, situated in the heart with its opening turned downward. (2.1)
Having raised [the seed-syllable] joined with the seed, which was previously placed upon a universal lotus—
therein, the supreme seed in the center consists of the essence of all Buddhas;
the Lord Lokeśvara is the staff, and the Master Vajradhara is the curved [scepter].
The limb is Samayavajra, while Ratnarāja is located at the head;
the two holders of the Buddha-vajra are proclaimed to be the bindu and the nāda.
[It is] covered by a family of radiating rays, stainless like the light of the autumn moon.
Thus should the wise one reflect, if he desires all accomplishments; by means of the conceptualization of self and other, he can never be obstructed. 4.14
One who follows the mantra, possesses firm instruction,
and is free from anger, having thoroughly examined the state of being,
indeed turns away from the desire for worldly existence.
He indeed aspires to the path of the Lord of Sages.
Māra arises from one's own mind alone; therefore, bring the mind under control.
For one who has brought their own mind under control, there is neither Māra nor any enemies.
Just as a bee, greedy for the fragrance of filaments within the heart of a lotus,
becomes trapped when the sun has set and suffers manifold misery;
so too, when the excellent teacher, the sun, has set, sentient beings [suffer].
Bound by the snares of pleasure within the terrible darkness of saṃsāra,
those who follow the path and perceive the way of reality as marked by the [proper] time reach the supreme state of Śiva upon its dawning.
Just as one who desires according to his wishes seeks only enjoyment while eating,
so too does he perceive existence as empty when it is being meditated upon.
That which is the reality of the Four Seats (Catuṣpīṭha), established within the four wheels—
This was written by the master Jitāri as something to be personally realized.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the "Ascertainment of the Perfect Awakening to the Wisdom of Prajñā," of the *Catuṣpīṭha*.

Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Rudra, Yasvini, ha ha, vihāri, huru huru svāhā! By binding a dead man’s tooth with this mantra upon one's hand, one may eat even the *sthālīpāka* (cooked sacrificial rice) wherever one desires; there one transfers [the power]. Through practice, the sign of success is seen.

*a* on the thumb; *ā* on the shank; *i* on the chest; *ī* on the private parts; *u* on the navel; *ū* on the abdomen; *ṛ* on the pair of breasts; *ṝ* on the pair of hands; *ḷ* on the throat; *ḹ* on the head; *e* on the pair of cheeks; *ai* on the two eyes; *o* on the pair of ears; again *o* on the head; *aṃ* and *aḥ* on all parts of the body. This is the explanation of the sixteen digits (*ṣoḍaśī-kalā*).
